_comment: Guided tour for the FCS confocal calculator. The UI is a declarative AutoForm view (fcs_calculator.view.json), so steps target bound attributes and the custom sections' keys. The tool takes no data and recomputes live, so the awaited step is an edit (a spin box's valueChanged) rather than a Run button. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: Seven numbers that are not independent
steps.text:
τ, D, rₕ, S, V_eff, N and c are tied together by four relations. Fix what you know and the rest follows:

τ_D = w_xy²/(4·D) · V_eff = π^{3/2}·w_xy³·S · D = k_BT/(6πη·rₕ) · c = N/(V_eff·N_A)

This tool takes no data. It is the arithmetic an FCS fit leaves you holding — and that arithmetic is where FCS numbers usually go wrong.

Seven steps.

steps.title: One degree of freedom, and you choose it
steps.text:
Pin D, rₕ or V_eff; the other two become outputs. Everything else on the page reads differently depending on which is lit.

This is worth checking before quoting anything: the value you think you are reading may be one the calculator just computed from the other two.

steps.title: Type the τ your fit gave you
steps.text:
This is the number FCS actually measures — the correlation time.

Everything else on the page is a conversion away from it, which is precisely the point of the next step.

await.hint: Type a correlation time in τ (µs) — anything will do.

steps.title: The calibration is the measurement
steps.text:
FCS measures τ. It does not measure D. Converting one to the other needs the beam waist w_xy, and w_xy comes from a calibration on a dye of known D — this panel.

Every quantity downstream inherits that calibration's error, and not equally:
• rₕ goes as 1/D — a 10 % calibration error is 10 %;
• V_eff goes as w_xy³ — the same 10 % is 33 %;
• c is proportional to 1/V_eff, so it carries that 33 % too.

That cube is why FCS concentrations are routinely quoted with more confidence than they have earned. Scale the reference to your temperature and viscosity before it is used — the panel does this — because comparing an uncorrected reference against a corrected measurement is a silent systematic.

steps.title: S is the other half of the volume, and usually a guess
steps.text:
S = w_z/w_xy is the focus's axial-to-lateral aspect ratio, typically 3–6 — and it is poorly determined by a fit, because the axial dimension barely shows in the correlation curve.

V_eff is linear in S. Choosing 5 when the truth is 3 is a 67 % error in every volume and every concentration that follows from it.

Fit it when the data support it, use a calibrated value when they do not, and quote whichever you did.

steps.title: D scales as T/η, and η moves fast
steps.text:
Water roughly halves in viscosity between 10 °C and 40 °C, so a D measured at room temperature and a literature D at 20 °C are not comparable numbers.

Use water η(T) takes the viscosity from an empirical relation. Override it whenever the sample is not water — glycerol, a crowded lysate, a membrane — because no temperature correction will discover an effective viscosity for you.

steps.title: rₕ is not a radius, and c is only as good as V_eff
steps.text:
Stokes–Einstein returns the radius of the sphere that would diffuse the way your molecule does. For anything elongated that number is larger than the molecule's own dimensions, and reading it as "size" overstates it.

The shape panel inverts the relation for the case you name — ellipsoid applies the Perrin friction factor, cylinder the Hansen approximation. None of them measures shape: they convert a measured D into a size given an assumption that stays yours.

And the concentration: it is N divided by V_eff, so it inherits the whole calibration chain above. If the number that matters is a concentration, the calibration is not a preliminary — it is the measurement.

Export the state to JSON when a number goes into a figure. The relations are cheap to recompute; the assumptions behind them are what you will want back in six months. The ? button has the rest.
